card_summary: Bead for bead: how the molecules in our Rx formulas compare by size, and why the word alone tells you so little.
headline: What is a peptide, *really*?
lede: A peptide is a short chain of amino acids, the same building blocks that make up proteins. The difference is length. Here's how the molecules you'll see at Equilibria compare, bead for bead.
recognition: Peptides are suddenly everywhere: in skincare, on podcasts, in the group chat. The same word gets used for a face cream and an injection, which makes it hard to know what you're actually looking at.
reframe: Size is the simplest way in. Each bead below is one amino acid. Count the beads and you know what kind of molecule you're dealing with. You'll also see why the word *peptide* on its own tells you so little.
viz_intro: One bead is one amino acid, and each full line holds 40. That's the FDA's cutoff: a chain longer than 40 counts as a protein.
viz_alt: Rows of beads, one per amino acid. KPV and GHK have 3, PT-141 has 7, oxytocin 9, BPC-157 15, MOTS-c 16, tirzepatide 39, insulin 51 and serum albumin 585, shown truncated. A dotted line marks 40. NAD+ and naltrexone sit off the string as single small molecules.
viz_caption: Plum beads: in an Equilibria Rx formula. Gold beads: shown for scale. Tap any row for detail.

scale_rows.row_note: A three-bead fragment from the end of a longer hormone called alpha-MSH.
The peptide in GHK-Cu: three beads paired with copper, first isolated from human plasma in 1973. In Radiance Cream Rx and Copper Glow Cream Rx.

Also called bremelanotide. Seven beads, six of them closed into a ring, including two building blocks you won't find in everyday proteins. Part of Intimacy Melt Rx, a compounded preparation that isn't an FDA-approved product.
Nine beads, with a small ring formed by two linked building blocks. Part of Intimacy Melt Rx.
A lab-made chain of fifteen, described as derived from a protein in gastric juice. In Gut Peptides Rx and Wolverine Recovery Rx.
Sixteen beads, coded in mitochondrial DNA rather than nuclear DNA.
Thirty-nine beads, just under the FDA's 40-bead line, so it's regulated as a peptide rather than a protein. Used in our compounded GLP/GIP Rx options, which aren't FDA-approved products.
Two chains of 21 and 30 beads, counted together. That puts insulin over the line, so the FDA regulates it as a protein. Shown for scale.
A blood protein, 585 beads long once it's fully made. It's here so you can see what a full-size protein looks like next to a peptide. Shown for scale.
NAD+ isn't made of amino acids at all. It's a dinucleotide, two nucleotides joined together. The active ingredient in Energy Spray Rx.
A classic small-molecule medicine, and the active ingredient in LDN Rx.

scale_takeaways_title: Three things the beads tell you

scale_takeaways.step_body: The word tells you a molecule is a short chain. It doesn't tell you what the chain does, how well it's been studied, or whether it suits you. That's what each explainer is for.

scale_takeaways.step_title: Length is only the first detail
scale_takeaways.step_body: Some short chains are closed into rings, like PT-141 and oxytocin. Some are paired with something else, like the copper in GHK-Cu.

scale_takeaways.step_title: Not every Rx is a peptide
scale_takeaways.step_body: NAD+ and naltrexone are small molecules, not chains. If someone calls everything in this category a peptide, you now know better.

cta_note: Each explainer covers what a molecule does, how strong the evidence is, and what a clinician will want to know.
